Sizes in the title graphic: Indohyus \~1 m and Pakicetus wolf-sized (\~1.8 m) (Thewissen et al. 2007, 2001); Ambulocetus \~3 m (Thewissen et al. 1994); Rodhocetus \~3 m (Gingerich et al. 1994); Dorudon \~5 m (Uhen 2004); Basilosaurus \~16–18 m (Gingerich et al. 1990); blue whale up to \~30 m. Ages as on the timeline slide.

<!-- 1b · the whole pathway -->
## From the first cells to whales: four billion years, two changes of element. {data-ref="Knoll 2015 Life on a Young Planet; Erwin et al. 2011 Science 334:1091; Shu et al. 1999 Nature 402:42; Benton 2015; Clack 2012; Uhen 2010"}

::: {.kicker}
The whole road · sea → land → sea
:::

<p class="caption" style="text-align:left;margin-top:0">Of the ~4 billion years, whales' ancestors spent all but ~325 million in water: a marine lineage that went ashore, then came back.</p>

::: {.notes}
Ages: earliest convincing fossil life \~3.5 Ga (stromatolites and microfossils; Knoll, A.H. (2015) Life on a Young Planet, Princeton University Press); eukaryotes by \~1.8–1.6 Ga (Knoll 2015); earliest animals \~575 Ma in the Ediacaran (Erwin, D.H. et al. (2011) "The Cambrian conundrum: early divergence and later ecological success in the early history of animals", Science 334:1091–1097); earliest vertebrates \~518 Ma, Chengjiang (Shu, D.-G. et al. (1999) "Lower Cambrian vertebrates from south China", Nature 402:42–46); lobe-finned fishes (sarcopterygians) by \~420 Ma, tetrapods \~375 Ma, amniotes \~315 Ma, mammaliaforms \~205 Ma, artiodactyls \~55 Ma (Benton 2015; Clack 2012); whales \~50 Ma (Uhen 2010). Living cetacean species: about 90 (Committee on Taxonomy, Society for Marine Mammalogy).
:::

<!-- 2 · where whales sit -->
## Whales are even-toed ungulates. Their closest living relatives are hippos. {data-ref="Nikaido, Rooney & Okada 1999 PNAS 96:10261; Gatesy 1997 MBE 14:537; Gingerich et al. 2001 Science 293:2239"}

::: {.kicker}
Where whales sit on the tree of life
:::

::: {.backdrop}
<div class="wash light" style="left:900px;top:420px;width:420px;height:320px;"></div>
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Cetaceans nest **inside Artiodactyla** (pigs, camels, ruminants, hippos) — hence the name [Cetartiodactyla]{.accent}.
- Molecular evidence: shared **SINE retroposon insertions** found only in whales and hippos (Nikaido et al. 1999) — near-irreversible markers of common ancestry.
- Fossil confirmation: early whales *Rodhocetus* and *Artiocetus* have the artiodactyl **double-pulley astragalus** (ankle bone) (Gingerich et al. 2001).
- The whale + hippo clade is called [Whippomorpha]{.accent}.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
<svg viewBox="0 0 520 300" width="520" height="300" aria-label="Cladogram: within Artiodactyla, hippos are the sister group of cetaceans" style="font-family:inherit">

  </g>

:::
:::
:::

(1999) "Phylogenetic relationships among cetartiodactyls based on insertions of short and long interspersed elements: hippopotamuses are the closest extant relatives of whales", PNAS 96:10261–10266. Gatesy, J. (1997) "More DNA support for a Cetacea/Hippopotamidae clade", Molecular Biology and Evolution 14:537–543. Gingerich, P.D., ul Haq, M., Zalmout, I.S., Khan, I.H. & Malkani, M.S. (2001) "Origin of whales from early artiodactyls: hands and feet of Eocene Protocetidae from Pakistan", Science 293:2239–2242.
:::

<!-- 2b · leaving the water -->
## Whales descend from fish that crawled out \~375 million years ago. {data-ref="Daeschler, Shubin & Jenkins 2006 Nature 440:757; Coates & Clack 1990 Nature 347:66; Niedźwiedzki et al. 2010 Nature 463:43; Clack 2012"}

::: {.kicker}
Before the return · leaving the water
:::

::: {.backdrop}
<div class="wash light" style="left:-100px;top:420px;width:520px;height:340px;"></div>
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- In the **Late Devonian**, lobe-finned fish related to today's lungfish and coelacanths gave rise to the first four-limbed vertebrates, the [tetrapods]{.accent}.
- *Tiktaalik roseae* (\~375 Ma, Ellesmere Island): a flat-headed fish with a **neck**, ribs, spiracles and robust fins with wrist-like bones — it could prop itself up in the shallows (Daeschler et al. 2006).
- *Acanthostega* and *Ichthyostega* (\~365 Ma, Greenland): true limbs with **eight and seven digits**, yet still largely aquatic — limbs evolved in water before they were used on land (Coates & Clack 1990).
- Trackways from Zachełmie, Poland, suggest limbed animals walking as early as \~395 Ma (Niedźwiedzki et al. 2010).
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.card}
**The reverse of the whale story.** The fish-to-tetrapod transition moved the same equipment the other way: paired fins became weight-bearing limbs with digits; the skull separated from the shoulder to make a neck; lungs, inherited from bony-fish ancestors, took over from gills; the ear was rebuilt for airborne sound. Whales later undid much of this — and kept the lungs.
:::

::: {.caption}
Air breathing predates land: lungs are an old bony-fish feature, still present in lungfish.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Daeschler, E.B., Shubin, N.H. & Jenkins, F.A. Jr (2006) "A Devonian tetrapod-like fish and the evolution of the tetrapod body plan", Nature 440:757–763; Shubin, N.H., Daeschler, E.B. & Jenkins, F.A. Jr (2006) "The pectoral fin of Tiktaalik roseae and the origin of the tetrapod limb", Nature 440:764–771. Coates, M.I. & Clack, J.A. (1990) "Polydactyly in the earliest known tetrapod limbs", Nature 347:66–69. Niedźwiedzki, G., Szrek, P., Narkiewicz, K., Narkiewicz, M. & Ahlberg, P.E. (2010) "Tetrapod trackways from the early Middle Devonian period of Poland", Nature 463:43–48. Clack, J.A. (2012) Gaining Ground: The Origin and Evolution of Tetrapods, 2nd ed., Indiana University Press. Cloutier, R. et al. (2020) "Elpistostege and the origin of the vertebrate hand", Nature 579:549–554 (digit-like bones inside a fin).
:::

<!-- 2c · the long way round -->
## From the Devonian shallows to the Eocene shore: the long way round. {data-ref="Benton 2015 Vertebrate Palaeontology; Clack 2012; Uhen 2010"}

::: {.kicker}
Before the return · 325 million years on land
:::

<svg viewBox="0 0 1200 300" width="1040" height="260" aria-label="Timeline from the first tetrapods (375 million years ago) through amniotes, mammals and artiodactyls to the first whales (50 million years ago)" style="font-family:inherit">
  <defs><linearGradient id="tl2" x1="0" x2="1"><stop offset="0" stop-color="#8ec1e0"></stop><stop offset=".18" stop-color="#c3703a"></stop><stop offset=".92" stop-color="#c3703a"></stop><stop offset="1" stop-color="#1d4f74"></stop></linearGradient></defs>
  <rect x="60" y="150" width="1080" height="10" rx="5" fill="url(#tl2)"></rect>
  <g stroke="#17303f" stroke-width="2">
    <line x1="60" y1="90" x2="60" y2="150"></line><line x1="240" y1="210" x2="240" y2="150"></line><line x1="560" y1="90" x2="560" y2="150"></line>
    <line x1="960" y1="210" x2="960" y2="150"></line><line x1="1000" y1="90" x2="1000" y2="150"></line><line x1="1060" y1="210" x2="1060" y2="150"></line>
  </g>
  <g font-size="17" fill="#17303f" text-anchor="middle">
    <text x="60" y="60" font-weight="700">First tetrapods</text><text x="60" y="82" font-size="14" fill="#4f6b7d">~375 Ma · Devonian</text>
    <text x="240" y="238" font-weight="700">Amniotes</text><text x="240" y="258" font-size="14" fill="#4f6b7d">~315 Ma · eggs that can be laid on land</text>
    <text x="560" y="60" font-weight="700">Mammaliaforms</text><text x="560" y="82" font-size="14" fill="#4f6b7d">~205 Ma · Late Triassic</text>
    <text x="930" y="238" text-anchor="end" font-weight="700">End-Cretaceous extinction</text><text x="930" y="258" text-anchor="end" font-size="14" fill="#4f6b7d">66 Ma · placental mammals radiate</text>
    <text x="1000" y="60" font-weight="700">First artiodactyls</text><text x="1000" y="82" font-size="14" fill="#4f6b7d">~55 Ma</text>
    <text x="1090" y="238" font-weight="700">Pakicetus</text><text x="1090" y="258" font-size="14" fill="#4f6b7d">~50 Ma · back to the water</text>
  </g>
  <g font-size="13" fill="#4f6b7d" text-anchor="middle"><text x="60" y="182">375 Ma</text><text x="600" y="182">on land (amber)</text><text x="1140" y="182">today</text></g>
</svg>

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Every mammal, bird and reptile alive today is a tetrapod: the ancestors of whales spent roughly **325 million years as land animals** before turning back.
- On the way they acquired what whales still carry: the **amniotic egg** (later, live birth), **warm blood**, **milk**, and the mammalian middle ear — three tiny bones whales rebuilt for hearing under water.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.card}
**So the whale pathway is water → land → water.** The return took \~10 million years; the stay on land took thirty times longer. That is why a whale's blueprint — lungs, warm blood, live birth, suckling, a few whiskers on the snout — is a land mammal's, redeployed (whales even lost their skin glands).
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Dates are conventional first-appearance ages: earliest tetrapods (Devonian, \~375–365 Ma), earliest amniotes (Carboniferous, \~315 Ma, e.g. Hylonomus), earliest mammaliaforms (Late Triassic, \~205 Ma, e.g. Morganucodon), earliest artiodactyls (early Eocene, \~55 Ma, e.g. Diacodexis) — see Benton, M.J. (2015) Vertebrate Palaeontology, 4th ed., Wiley-Blackwell, and Clack (2012). Whale dates as on the following slides (Uhen 2010). Middle ear: the mammalian malleus and incus derive from jaw bones of earlier amniotes; in whales the ear bones are isolated in a dense bulla for underwater hearing (Nummela et al. 2004).
:::

<!-- 3 · timeline -->
## The transition happened fast: from wading to fully marine in about ten million years. {data-ref="Uhen 2010; Marx, Lambert & Uhen 2016; Slater, Goldbogen & Pyenson 2017"}

::: {.kicker}
Fifty-three million years in one line
:::

<!-- 4 · Indohyus -->
## *Indohyus*: the raoellids, sister group of whales. {data-ref="Thewissen et al. 2007 Nature 450:1190"}

::: {.kicker}
Transition 1 · a wading relative
:::

::: {.backdrop}
<div class="wash" style="left:820px;top:120px;width:460px;height:380px;"></div>
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Raccoon-sized artiodactyl from the **middle Eocene of Kashmir, India** (\~48 Ma), described from a skeleton in 2007.
- Shares with whales the **involucrum**: a thickened wall of the auditory bulla otherwise found only in cetaceans.
- Heavy, **osteosclerotic** limb bones (ballast, as in hippos and otters) and oxygen isotopes of teeth indicate time spent in water.
- Teeth suggest a plant-based or omnivorous diet — the first step into water was **not** about hunting fish.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.card}
**Why it matters.** *Indohyus* shows that aquatic habits (wading, hiding in water) preceded the dietary and locomotor changes seen in true whales; the ear came first.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Thewissen, J.G.M., Cooper, L.N., Clementz, M.T., Bajpai, S. & Tiwari, B.N. (2007) "Whales originated from aquatic artiodactyls in the Eocene epoch of India", Nature 450:1190–1194.
:::

<!-- 5 · Pakicetus -->
## *Pakicetus* (\~50 Ma): a whale that walked on four legs. {data-ref="Gingerich et al. 1983 Science 220:403; Thewissen et al. 2001 Nature 413:277"}

::: {.kicker}
Transition 2 · the earliest whales
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Early Eocene of **Pakistan** (Kuldana Formation); first described from a skull in 1983, skeletons in 2001.
- Wolf-sized, long-snouted, with eyes set high on the skull; limbs built for land and shallow water — **not** a swimmer's body.
- Recognised as a cetacean by its **ear** (involucrum, pachyosteosclerotic bulla) and teeth, long before its body was known.
- Ankle bones with the artiodactyl **double-pulley astragalus**: the fossil and molecular stories agree.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

<!-- 6 · Ambulocetus -->
## *Ambulocetus natans* (\~49 Ma): an ambush predator at the water's edge. {data-ref="Thewissen, Hussain & Arif 1994 Science 263:210; Nummela et al. 2004 Nature 430:776"}

::: {.kicker}
Transition 3 · the walking, swimming whale
:::

::: {.backdrop}
<div class="wash light" style="left:-80px;top:380px;width:520px;height:360px;"></div>
:::

- About **3 m long**, from the early–middle Eocene of Pakistan; large hind feet and a powerful tail suggest swimming by **pelvic paddling and undulation**, like an otter.
- Could still support itself on land; crocodile-like ecology inferred from skull shape and stable isotopes (fresh to brackish water).
- Hearing: early whales had a **mandibular fat pad** pathway for underwater sound, while pakicetids still heard mostly in air (Nummela et al. 2004).

<div class="card" style="position:absolute;left:720px;top:470px;width:500px;">
  <p><strong>Naming.</strong> <em>Ambulocetus natans</em> = "the walking whale that swims" — the name says exactly what the skeleton shows.</p>
</div>

::: {.notes}
Thewissen, J.G.M., Hussain, S.T. & Arif, M. (1994) "Fossil evidence for the origin of aquatic locomotion in archaeocete whales", Science 263:210–212. Nummela, S., Thewissen, J.G.M., Bajpai, S., Hussain, S.T. & Kumar, K. (2004) "Eocene evolution of whale hearing", Nature 430:776–778.
:::

<!-- 7 · Protocetids -->
## Protocetids: seagoing whales that still gave birth on land. {data-ref="Gingerich et al. 1994 Nature 368:844; Gingerich et al. 2009 PLoS ONE 4:e4366; Lambert et al. 2019 Curr Biol 29:1352"}

::: {.kicker}
Transition 4 · going to sea
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- *Rodhocetus* (\~47 Ma, Pakistan): shortened neck, robust tail, hind limbs still weight-bearing (Gingerich et al. 1994).
- *Maiacetus inuus* (\~47.5 Ma): a female preserved with a near-term **fetus positioned head-first** — modern whales are born tail-first — implying birth on land (Gingerich et al. 2009).
- *Peregocetus pacificus* (\~42.6 Ma, Peru): a four-legged whale on the Pacific coast of South America, showing protocetids had **crossed the Atlantic** by the middle Eocene (Lambert et al. 2019).
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
| Genus | Age | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Rodhocetus* | \~47 Ma | Pakistan |
| *Maiacetus* | \~47.5 Ma | Pakistan |
| *Georgiacetus* | \~40 Ma | SE United States |
| *Peregocetus* | \~42.6 Ma | Peru |

::: {.caption}
Ages as reported in the describing papers.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Gingerich, P.D., Raza, S.M., Arif, M., Anwar, M. & Zhou, X. (1994) "New whale from the Eocene of Pakistan and the origin of cetacean swimming", Nature 368:844–847. Gingerich, P.D., ul-Haq, M., von Koenigswald, W., Sanders, W.J., Smith, B.H. & Zalmout, I.S. (2009) "New protocetid whale from the middle Eocene of Pakistan: birth on land, precocial development, and sexual dimorphism", PLoS ONE 4(2):e4366. Lambert, O., Bianucci, G., Salas-Gismondi, R., Di Celma, C., Steurbaut, E., Urbina, M. & de Muizon, C. (2019) "An amphibious whale from the middle Eocene of Peru reveals early South Pacific dispersal of quadrupedal cetaceans", Current Biology 29:1352–1359. Georgiacetus: Hulbert, R.C. et al. (1998) Journal of Paleontology 72:907–927.
:::

<!-- 8 · Basilosaurids -->
## Basilosaurids (\~41–34 Ma): whales that could no longer leave the water. {data-ref="Gingerich, Smith & Simons 1990 Science 249:154; Uhen 2004 Univ. Michigan Papers on Paleontology 34"}

::: {.kicker}
Transition 5 · fully aquatic
:::

::: {.backdrop}
<div class="wash deep" style="left:640px;top:-60px;width:720px;height:420px;"></div>
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- *Basilosaurus* (up to \~17–18 m, eel-like body) and *Dorudon* (\~5 m): fully marine, with tail flukes and flipper-like forelimbs.
- Tiny but complete **hind limbs** preserved in *Basilosaurus isis* — with knee, ankle and toes — too small to bear weight (Gingerich et al. 1990).
- Nostrils have moved back along the snout; the pelvis is no longer attached to the spine.
- Best known from **Wadi Al-Hitan** ("Valley of Whales"), Egypt — a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2005.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

The hind limb (small triangle near the tail) is a few percent of body length.
:::
:::

:::

<!-- 9 · body plan -->
## The anatomical checklist of becoming a whale. {data-ref="Thewissen et al. 2006 PNAS 103:8414; Thewissen et al. 2009"}

::: {.kicker}
What actually changed
:::

| Trait | Land ancestor | Modern whale | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Nostrils | tip of snout | blowhole on top of head | progressive migration through protocetids and basilosaurids |
| Hearing | air-borne, via eardrum | water-borne, via jaw fat pad and isolated bulla | involucrum already in raoellids; fat pad in ambulocetids |
| Forelimb | walking leg | flipper, fingers encased | protocetids keep flexible elbows; basilosaurids lose them |
| Hind limb | weight-bearing | vestigial pelvis, no external limb | *Sonic hedgehog* signalling shuts down in the dolphin hind-limb bud (Thewissen et al. 2006) |
| Tail | balance | horizontal fluke, main propulsor | flattened tail vertebrae in basilosaurids |
| Pelvis | fused to sacrum | free-floating | sacrum lost by the basilosaurid stage |

::: {.notes}
Thewissen, J.G.M., Cohn, M.J., Stevens, L.S., Bajpai, S., Heyning, J. & Horton, W.E. Jr (2006) "Developmental basis for hind-limb loss in dolphins and origin of the cetacean bodyplan", PNAS 103:8414–8418. Thewissen et al. (2009) Evolution: Education and Outreach 2:272–288 (review of the anatomical sequence).
:::

<!-- 10 · Neoceti / mysticetes -->
## Baleen whales began with teeth. {data-ref="Lambert et al. 2017 Curr Biol 27:1535; Geisler et al. 2017 Curr Biol 27:2036; Fordyce & Marx 2018 Curr Biol 28:1670"}

::: {.kicker}
Transition 6 · the great split
:::

::: {.backdrop}
<div class="wash light" style="left:840px;top:380px;width:480px;height:360px;"></div>
:::

- Around **36–34 Ma** the crown group [Neoceti]{.accent} splits into Mysticeti (baleen whales) and Odontoceti (toothed whales).
- *Mystacodon selenensis* (36.4 Ma, Peru) is the oldest known mysticete — and it has **teeth**, with wear suggesting suction feeding (Lambert et al. 2017).
- *Coronodon havensteini* (Oligocene, South Carolina) apparently **filtered with its teeth**, using slots between them (Geisler et al. 2017).
- Aetiocetids had teeth plus, in some interpretations, incipient baleen; *Llanocetus* (\~34 Ma, Antarctica) was already toothed and large (Fordyce & Marx 2018).
- Baleen itself rarely fossilises; its presence is inferred from **nutrient foramina** on the palate.

::: {.notes}
Lambert, O., Martínez-Cáceres, M., Bianucci, G., Di Celma, C., Salas-Gismondi, R., Steurbaut, E., Urbina, M. & de Muizon, C. (2017) "Earliest mysticete from the late Eocene of Peru sheds new light on the origin of baleen whales", Current Biology 27:1535–1541. Geisler, J.H., Boessenecker, R.W., Brown, M. & Beatty, B.L. (2017) "The origin of filter feeding in whales", Current Biology 27:2036–2042. Fordyce, R.E. & Marx, F.G. (2018) "Gigantism precedes filter feeding in baleen whale evolution", Current Biology 28:1670–1676.
:::

<!-- 11 · echolocation -->
## Toothed whales evolved echolocation early. {data-ref="Geisler et al. 2014 Nature 508:383; Churchill et al. 2016 Curr Biol 26:2144"}

::: {.kicker}
Transition 7 · seeing with sound
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- *Cotylocara macei* (\~28 Ma, South Carolina) shows a skull with **asymmetry and deep air sinuses** — the bony correlates of a sound-producing nasal apparatus (Geisler et al. 2014).
- *Echovenator sandersi* (Oligocene) had a cochlea adapted to **ultrasonic hearing**, indicating high-frequency hearing arose at or near the base of Odontoceti (Churchill et al. 2016).
- Modern toothed whales produce clicks with **phonic lips** in the nasal passages, focus them through the melon, and receive echoes through the fat-filled lower jaw.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.card}
**Two strategies, one ancestor.** Within a few million years of the Neoceti split, one lineage was screening prey out of water, the other was ranging it with sound. Both are solutions to feeding in an ocean where the eyes are of limited use.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Geisler, J.H., Colbert, M.W. & Carew, J.L. (2014) "A new fossil species supports an early origin for toothed whale echolocation", Nature 508:383–386. Churchill, M., Martínez-Cáceres, M., de Muizon, C., Mnieckowski, J. & Geisler, J.H. (2016) "The origin of high-frequency hearing in whales", Current Biology 26:2144–2149.
:::

<!-- 12 · gigantism -->
## Whales were not always giants. Gigantism is geologically recent. {data-ref="Slater, Goldbogen & Pyenson 2017 Proc R Soc B 284:20170546; Goldbogen et al. 2019 Science 366:1367"}

::: {.kicker}
Transition 8 · becoming enormous
:::

::: {.backdrop}
<div class="wash deep" style="left:-160px;top:80px;width:640px;height:520px;"></div>
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Body-size analysis of living and fossil baleen whales shows very large size (> 10 m) evolving **independently in several lineages within the last \~4.5 million years** (Slater et al. 2017).
- The proposed driver: Plio-Pleistocene cooling and wind-driven **coastal upwelling** concentrated prey into dense seasonal patches, rewarding lunge-feeders that travel far and eat in bulk.
- The blue whale, up to \~30 m and well over 100 tonnes, is the largest animal known to have lived; energetic measurements suggest filter-feeding sizes are capped by the cost of a lunge (Goldbogen et al. 2019).
:::

    <rect x="560" y="370" width="240" height="46" rx="8" fill="#fff" fill-opacity=".7" stroke="#c9d9e4"></rect><text x="572" y="390" font-weight="700">Saliva · SLC4A9</text><text x="572" y="408" font-size="12" fill="#4f6b7d">no need to moisten food under water</text>
    <rect x="820" y="370" width="240" height="46" rx="8" fill="#fff" fill-opacity=".7" stroke="#c9d9e4"></rect><text x="832" y="390" font-weight="700">DNA repair · POLM</text><text x="832" y="408" font-size="12" fill="#4f6b7d">an error-prone repair enzyme, dropped</text>
  </g>
  <g stroke="#c9d9e4" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="3 3">
    <line x1="450" y1="90" x2="450" y2="300"></line><line x1="710" y1="90" x2="620" y2="300"></line><line x1="970" y1="90" x2="690" y2="300"></line>

Gene examples and interpretations from Huelsmann et al. (2019): AANAT and ASMT (melatonin synthesis; cetaceans show unihemispheric sleep), F12 and KLKB1 (contact activation pathway of blood clotting; loss may reduce thrombosis risk during diving), KLK8 (epidermal function; cetacean skin lacks hair and glands), SLC4A9 (salivary bicarbonate secretion), POLM (DNA polymerase μ, error-prone repair). McGowen et al. (2020) for the living-cetacean phylogeny. Huelsmann, M., Hecker, N., Springer, M.S., Gatesy, J., Sharma, V. & Hiller, M. (2019) "Genes lost during the transition from land to water in cetaceans highlight genomic changes associated with aquatic adaptations", Science Advances 5:eaaw6671. McGowen, M.R. et al. (2020) "Phylogenomic resolution of the cetacean tree of life using target sequence capture", Systematic Biology 69:479–501.

<!-- 13b · not only whales -->
## Returning to the sea is a well-worn path: dozens of tetrapod lineages have done it. {data-ref="Kelley & Pyenson 2015 Science 348:aaa3716; Vermeij & Motani 2018 Paleobiology 44:237; Domning 2001; Rybczynski et al. 2009; Motani et al. 2015; Slack et al. 2006"}

::: {.kicker}
Not only whales
:::

::: {.backdrop}
<div class="wash light" style="left:880px;top:400px;width:460px;height:340px;"></div>
:::

| Lineage | Came from | Went back | Transitional fossil |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Whales** (Cetacea) | artiodactyl mammals | \~50 Ma | *Pakicetus*, *Ambulocetus* |
| **Sea cows** (Sirenia: manatees, dugongs) | afrotherian mammals, kin to elephants | \~48 Ma | *Pezosiren*, a four-legged sea cow from Jamaica (Domning 2001) |
| **Seals, sea lions, walrus** (Pinnipedia) | bear- and otter-like carnivorans | \~24 Ma | *Puijila*, a web-footed Arctic otter-like form (Rybczynski et al. 2009) |
| **Ichthyosaurs** † | reptiles, after the end-Permian extinction | \~248 Ma | *Cartorhynchus*, short-snouted, amphibious (Motani et al. 2015) |
| **Plesiosaurs** † and kin | reptiles (sauropterygians) | Triassic | placodonts, nothosaurs |
| **Mosasaurs** † | lizards | \~100 Ma | early forms with walking limbs |
| **Sea turtles** | turtles | Early Cretaceous | — |
| **Penguins** | flying seabirds | \~60 Ma | *Waimanu*, New Zealand (Slack et al. 2006) |

::: {.cite}
Also: marine crocodiles (Jurassic), sea snakes (more than once), the Galápagos marine iguana, sea otters, polar bears; and, semi-aquatic, the hippos. † = extinct. Ages are approximate first appearances.
:::

::: {.notes}
Kelley, N.P. & Pyenson, N.D. (2015) "Evolutionary innovation and ecology in marine tetrapods from the Triassic to the Anthropocene", Science 348:aaa3716 — review of the repeated invasions of the sea by amniotes. Vermeij, G.J. & Motani, R. (2018) "Land to sea transitions in vertebrates: the dynamics of colonization", Paleobiology 44:237–250. Domning, D.P. (2001) "The earliest known fully quadrupedal sirenian", Nature 413:625–627. Rybczynski, N., Dawson, M.R. & Tedford, R.H. (2009) "A semi-aquatic Arctic mammalian carnivore from the Miocene epoch and origin of Pinnipedia", Nature 458:1021–1024. Motani, R. et al. (2015) "A basal ichthyosauriform with a short snout from the Lower Triassic of China", Nature 517:485–488. Slack, K.E. et al. (2006) "Early penguin fossils, plus mitochondrial genomes, calibrate avian evolution", Molecular Biology and Evolution 23:1144–1155. Since all tetrapods descend from Devonian fish, every marine tetrapod lineage is a water → land → water story; whales are the one that went furthest.
:::

<!-- 13c · convergence -->
## Different ancestors, same solutions — and one whale-specific twist. {data-ref="Kelley & Pyenson 2015; Motani et al. 2014 PLoS ONE 9:e88640; Houssaye 2009 Integrative Zoology 4:325"}

::: {.kicker}
Not only whales · what the returns have in common
:::

::: {.backdrop}
<div class="wash deep" style="left:-140px;top:60px;width:520px;height:420px;"></div>
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Convergences

- **Streamlined body, tail propulsion**: ichthyosaurs, whales and tuna converged on the same outline; ichthyosaurs beat sideways like fish, whales up and down like running mammals.
- **Limbs → flippers**, often with extra finger bones (hyperphalangy) in ichthyosaurs, plesiosaurs and whales.
- **Dense bones first, light bones later**: early stages of many lineages show ballast-like thickened bone (whales, sea cows, early ichthyosaurs), replaced by lighter skeletons once they become fast open-water swimmers (Houssaye 2009).
- **Live birth**: ichthyosaurs gave birth tail-first at sea, like whales — and, judging by the earliest embryos, had acquired viviparity on land beforehand (Motani et al. 2014).
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Where whales differ

- Most returning lineages keep a foothold on land — seals, turtles and penguins still come ashore to breed. Whales and sea cows are among the few that **never leave the water**.
- Only toothed whales evolved **echolocation**; only baleen whales evolved **bulk filter feeding** at giant size.
- No known lineage has gone water → land → water → *land* again: once fully marine, the return ticket seems lost.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Kelley & Pyenson (2015) on convergence and ecological roles of marine tetrapods. Motani, R., Jiang, D.-Y., Tintori, A., Rieppel, O. & Chen, G.-B. (2014) "Terrestrial origin of viviparity in Mesozoic marine reptiles indicated by Early Triassic embryonic fossils", PLoS ONE 9:e88640. Houssaye, A. (2009) "'Pachyostosis' in aquatic amniotes: a review", Integrative Zoology 4:325–340. The statement that no lineage has returned to land after becoming fully marine reflects the fossil record as reviewed by Vermeij & Motani (2018); amphibious lineages (e.g. seals) are not counted as "fully marine".
:::

<!-- 14 · closing -->
# Ear first, then feet, then sound and size. {.break data-ref=synthesis}

::: {.backdrop}
<div class="wash" style="left:700px;top:120px;width:560px;height:460px;"></div>

<div class="wash warm" style="left:-100px;top:500px;width:420px;height:240px;"></div>
:::

::: {.sub}
Fish left the water once, \~375 million years ago; their descendants have gone back dozens of times. Whales are the lineage that went furthest, and the best documented: molecules, fossils and development all tell the same story, from Ellesmere Island to Kashmir to Peru.
:::

::: {.notes}
Closing synthesis; see the references slide. A good general-audience account: Pyenson, N.D. (2018) Spying on Whales, Viking; and Thewissen, J.G.M. (2014) The Walking Whales, University of California Press.
:::
